# The Tax Wedge in the Reform Estimates {#sec-app-fiscal-wedge}

A tax change can move reported materials shares mechanically, without any change in overreporting: prices and the tax paid on sales and purchases adjust to the new rates. The two-tax model isolates the part of this adjustment that runs through the sales-tax rates. With different rates on sales, $\tau_S$, and on purchases, $\tau_P$, the gross materials share carries the wedge $\ln\big((1-\tau_S)/(1-\tau_P)\big)$, which depends on the rates themselves. The 1983 reform changed those rates in the liable industries, so a rise in the gross share after the reform could reflect either more overreporting or this wedge. The event study in @sec-fiscal uses the share net of sales taxes, which removes the wedge.

@tbl-fiscal-wedge estimates the wedge's contribution directly: the same event study, with the gross minus the net share as the outcome. Its coefficients equal the gap between the event study on the gross share and on the net share. Before the reform the wedge does not move. After it, the wedge rises by about 0.006 to 0.008 for unincorporated firms in liable industries, roughly a tenth of their measured response, and by 0.011 to 0.013 for proprietorships in 1984--1986, most of their response in those years. An event study on the gross share would attribute this mechanical component to overreporting.
